why: Story 2 better establishes the roughly 70% collapse before the negative day and explicitly limits its conclusions to the two benchmarks observed. Its daily-versus-averages chart makes the smoothing effect immediately visible; both stories’ chart pairs support their prose, with identifiable series colours and directly labelled red negative-price highlights. Story 1 supplies the useful $54.34 gap and a later recovery milestone, but neither story establishes the gap’s historical rarity, clearly identifies when the decline accelerated, or compares earlier collapses adequately. Although the actual cause is outside the price data’s reach, both stories introduce a CFTC report outside the supplied inventory, so their causal accounts require verification against that report rather than acceptance as supplied evidence. Story 1 additionally relies on an unavailable ICE specification and needs its concluding “delivery deadline” distinguished from contract expiry.

reader_questions.q: Which oil price went below zero, on what date and by how much, and do these data measure spot prices or futures contracts?
What would make a seller pay someone to take oil, and what evidence would establish why that happened in April 2020?
How far had prices already fallen since the start of 2020, and when did the decline accelerate?
What happened to Brent when WTI went negative, and how unusual was the gap between them?
How many daily observations were negative, and how quickly did prices recover afterward?
How different does April 2020 look in the daily prices versus the weekly and monthly averages?
Was the negative price unprecedented in the available records, and how did the surrounding slump compare with earlier oil-price collapses?
